title: Decades-Old Disneyland Photos Spark Time Traveler Theory Online
content:
Disneyland has been photographed more than almost anywhere on earth, and that creates a specific opportunity.

Every day since 1955, thousands of people have aimed cameras at the same castle, the same storefronts, the same stretch of Main Street, U.S.A. Millions of those photos sit in shoeboxes, slide carousels, and undeveloped canisters in garages across the country. Everyone captured strangers in the background who never knew and never will.

Disneyland is sitting on one of the biggest accidental archives of ordinary people in existence.

Once in a while, somebody finds one of those strangers and cannot explain him.

How the Disneyland Photos Turned Up

Josie Weaver, 30, was visiting her grandparents for lunch while between jobs.

Her grandfather, Tom Eubank, 84, asked for help selling his old Canon camera.

That turned into a project. The two went hunting for film and a projector to see what the camera had actually captured.

Eubank told PEOPLE he first got the camera in 1963 aboard a Navy ship in the Mediterranean. He kept it through his deployment, photographing his uniform and the scenery on the Isle of Capri.

Woman Believes She Spots Time Traveler in Grandfather's Disneyland Photos from the 1960shttps://t.co/2NRU5PYpPP

— Disneyland News Today (@dlnt) September 16, 2026

Decades of film, mostly unexamined.

What Was on It

Among the images: photos from Eubank’s 1968 Disneyland trip.

The list reads like a time capsule:

  • The train station
  • 20,000 Leagues Under the Sea
  • Swiss Family Treehouse
  • it’s a small world
  • Pirates of the Caribbean
  • Sleeping Beauty Castle

That alone is worth an afternoon if you care about park history. 20,000 Leagues closed decades ago. The Swiss Family Treehouse became Tarzan’s Treehouse in 1999. Pirates had only opened in March 1967, so those shots catch it barely a year old.

But that is not what Weaver noticed.

The Man in New Orleans Square at Disneyland

One photo included someone who did not look like he belonged in 1968.

Weaver flagged his clothing, his sunglasses, and especially his haircut, all of which looked wrong for the era next to everyone around him.

“That was so funny because the picture popped up and he was like front and center,” she said. “And it just looked like someone that we would see out and about now. And he looked so different. To me, he looked so different to everyone around him, especially with his haircut. It was like faded on the side.”

The fade is what sells it.

Why the Haircut Does the Work

A faded cut reads as extremely contemporary, and that is exactly why this photo hits.

Men’s styles in 1968 ran longer at the sides or slicked back. The tapered fade filling barbershops today has a different silhouette, and it is one of the most reliable markers people use to date a photo without consciously thinking about it.

Drop that silhouette into a crowd of 1968 guests and your brain flags it before you can say why.

What People Think

The photo pulled more than 1,000 comments on TikTok.

Plenty agreed that he looks out of place. Others landed somewhere more grounded, suggesting he was just ahead of the times.

That second read is almost certainly correct.

Fashion never moved at one speed. In any crowd of a few hundred people in 1968, some dressed like 1968, some like 1958, and a few like something that would not go mainstream for another decade. Southern California ran ahead of the national curve.

Fades also are not a modern invention. Variations have existed in barbering for a long time, including in military grooming, which is relevant given Eubank was in the Navy.

Almost certainly not.

But this is the fun part, and there is no reason to be a killjoy.

Photos like this work because they briefly collapse the distance between now and then. A crowd of strangers from 1968 feels safely historical until one of them looks like he could be behind you in line at Starbucks. That single face makes the whole scene feel close, and close is unsettling in a way that far away never is.

He was almost certainly a guest at Disneyland on an ordinary day in 1968, wearing whatever he wanted, with no idea a camera behind him would make him internet-famous nearly sixty years later.

If he is still alive, he would be in his eighties now.

The Better Story

Honestly, the time-travel angle isn’t even the best part.

A man bought a camera on a Navy ship in 1963, carried it through a deployment, took it to Disneyland in 1968, then put the film away for over five decades. His granddaughter sat down to help him sell it and ended up looking at a version of Disneyland that no longer exists.

That is what old film does. Closed attractions, a changed park, and one stranger in New Orleans Square who has apparently been ahead of his time since 1968.

Source: PEOPLE interview with Josie Weaver and Tom Eubank.
